_comment: Portuguese profile (pt-BR voices). Voices: carolina (feminine), leo (masculine).
_localeComment: BCP-47 codes for Amazon Transcribe, which gives the coaching lane an independent transcript and identifies which language was actually spoken. Streaming identification needs at least two options, one dialect each.
_genderComment: Must match the voice: gendered languages conjugate self-reference. Feminine voices: tiffany, amy, olivia, kiara, ambre, beatrice, tina, lupe, carolina. Masculine: matthew, arjun, florian, lorenzo, lennart, carlos, leo.
regionalVariation: Brazilian "de" and "te" as dji/tchi versus European d/t
carioca "s" as sh at the end of a syllable
European reduction of unstressed vowels, which clips syllables English speakers expect to hear
word-initial "r" as an h-like sound in Brazil and a trill in Portugal
você versus tu, and the different verb endings that follow each
regional vocabulary across Brazil, Portugal and the African varieties
_learnerErrorsComment: The other side of the coin from regionalVariation: mistakes learners genuinely make that must NOT be excused as accent. Without these the reviewer treats almost everything as dialect and stays silent.
learnerErrors: replacing the nasal vowels of ão, ãe, õe with plain vowels
reducing unstressed vowels the way English does, past what the variety expects
reading initial "r" as an English r rather than an h-like sound or trill
reading "lh" and "nh" as plain l and n
pronunciationExample: your nasal "ão" in "pão" came out as a plain "a", so it sounded like "pa"
grammarExample: "eu fui ao mercado" — ir takes "a" plus the article, which contracts to "ao"
